content: The term Blue 88 refers to a blue-colored pill that was a combination of sedative medications, primarily barbiturates. This pharmaceutical was administered to American soldiers during the Second World War who were experiencing battle fatigue, a condition now more commonly referred to as combat stress reaction. Its primary purpose was to induce sleep and provide temporary relief from the psychological strain of combat. The use of this drug during World War II was highlighted in a 1994 episode of the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) series American Experience, specifically in the episode titled Battle of the Bulge. This documentary, produced by the WGBH Educational Foundation in Boston, Massachusetts, examined the critical German offensive in the Ardennes region of France during the winter of 1944-1945. The program also discussed the challenges faced by Allied forces, including the increasing number of soldiers suffering from battle fatigue. As the Ardennes Offensive progressed and Allied casualties mounted, there was a growing shortage of combat-ready soldiers. Those who were not severely injured or incapacitated by psychological trauma were often encouraged to return to the front lines. Captain Ben Kimmelman, a dental officer with the 4th Medical Battalion Special Troops of the 4th Infantry Division, was actively involved in the medical corps during this time. He personally observed the devastating psychological toll of the battle. According to Captain Kimmelman, approximately one in four soldiers wounded during the Battle of the Bulge were classified as psychiatric casualties, highlighting the significant mental health impact of the conflict. Later in the war, Captain Kimmelman, along with the rest of the 2-8 Infantry Regiment (commonly referred to as Easy Company), was captured by German forces during their campaign. Despite this, he survived the war.
